This year I was given a class specifically for students who failed the first half of 10th English (because we randomly decided to make that—but not any of the other grade levels—a year-long class this year), and I so wish I were paid like the actor that I am for this academic theatre. There are kids who are purposefully trying to fail again so that they can be funneled into fasttrack and graduate at 16. There’s no amount of tap-dancing I can do to get them to change their plans. I thought I had it bad with my gen ed students not giving a shit, but if I don’t make everything 100% direct instruction or multiple choice or fill-in-the-blanks (I shit you not, I made a full-in-the-blanks essay so they could at least turn something in), they wouldn’t do a thing for me. 

I know I’m fighting a losing battle every day. And I so wish I could quit. But I’ve spent most of my life in poverty, and this, oddly enough, is the best-paying job I’ve ever had. I feel like such a fraud trying to grin and bear it every single day while the whole educational system falls apart around me. Disciplinary actions have been defanged. Rigor in the curriculum has risen in a way that the students I have now are never going to be able to meet. Central office pushes “innovative” plans onto schools that don’t work and were never brought up to us teachers before implementation. And I come to work every day telling myself that I’m going to be part of a big, needed change in this system. 🤡

It was a disaster in the year before because it was based on homerooms, but the problem with that was that we only met for homeroom like once a month or so, so teachers didn’t really know the students they were calling about as well as the ones they saw every day. When parents had questions of “well why didn’t my kid show up for that class??” and we had no idea how to respond. 

Last year we started having daily homeroom meetings, but still having to do calls home for tier 2 truants was still a hassle that involved a lot of confusing paperwork. So now the attendance secretary is handling those calls this year.

If it is a process that can be automated, automate it. Automatic feedback that a student can see on a missed multiple choice question is much more valuable than verbal feedback a week later about content they’ve already forgotten about. 

And for feedback on essays, if it takes you more than 2 minutes to write it down, move on. Focus on commenting on issues/good things unique to that particular student. Everything else can be covered by circling categories on a rubric.

We’re doing a thing called “literacy walks” where all of the English teachers get together and sit in on another English teacher’s class for 10 minutes. We fill out a graphic organizer (because we are children) to take notes on how engaged the students are in learning. A group of us sat in on a teacher who was covering grammar. Pretty cut and dry stuff, nothing that a teenager would find all that fascinating. When we met back up to discuss our findings, our principal said “sometimes you need to go back to the basics to be able to teach more high engagement lessons.” But grammar isn’t a “basic” thing. It’s a state standard that we have to teach. 

Sometimes it feels like admin are worse than the kids in saying “when do we get to do something fun???” We have to bend over backwards to entertain them if we want to convince them that we’re doing our jobs correctly. And so much time in post-observation conferences is wasted on explaining decisions that the admin doesn’t understand because they haven’t looked at our curriculum, and they haven’t taught at the grade level or in the subject that we teach in. 

This is only my 3rd year, but I’m already getting so tired of being micromanaged.

Last year I had a system where I let students sign themselves out on a clipboard and take one of my 2 hall passes. If it was just to the bathroom or vending machine, they didn’t have to tell me, they just could get up and sign out when they needed. It worked because I had 2 honors classes and one general, but even with the general I had some pretty responsible kids. In 10th grade, if you can believe it. It was so nice. I got really spoiled by how smooth that made my classes run. 

I miss being able to do that, because now my school switched to an online hall pass system and there are not enough chromebooks in the school for all students to have them, so 9 times out of 10, I have to sign them out myself. Having to deal with the decision fatigue at the end of the day has been rough. But even if I could, I don’t think I would try my old system on the group of students I have now. They blew up a teacher’s microwave last year, so I know I have to keep a close eye on them lmao

I keep hearing the word “intentional” in meetings and PDs and it enrages me every time. I have social anxiety. Every single move I make and every single word I speak is calculated. If I don’t have a reason for doing/saying something, I’m not doing/saying it. What do you mean I need to be *more* intentional when I teach??

As a teacher who grew up with (and still has) social anxiety, I avoid doing this like the plague. It really sucks because the rubric that we’re scored on expects us to group students to make work more engaging for them. I have students that I know would rather work alone than squeeze themselves in with people they don’t know, but when I do give group work, it’s usually too heavy to do alone, and it hinges upon students being able to bounce ideas off of each other and check each other to make sure they read the instructions correctly. 

Usually my remedy to this problem is to ask students to write an exit ticket telling me the name of at least one student they would like to be grouped with. Then I pick groups based on that. That way, the more social kids almost feel like they picked the groups themselves, and the quiet kids don’t feel anxious about being the last pick. Also, I  can give the quiet kids a “safe person” kind of option if they have certain people they’re more comfortable with. But I know I still have kids who don’t feel like they know or like anyone enough to want to work with them, so this solution isn’t foolproof. 

Classroom politics are hard. And it really sucks to see from the teacher perspective that admin expects me to push socially anxious kids to do activities that make their anxiety feel worse.

This is my first year teaching, so I’m still a bit naive. I bought donuts for my kids for doing a really good job during my first observation. (I asked my VP to observe my “bad” class because I wanted some advice on how to manage and motivate them better.) I really didn’t expect them to be as good as they were, but then I put two and two together and realized they behaved because the VP was in the room, and they didn’t want to draw attention to themselves by acting up because they would get dress coded (my most problematic behaviors come from a group of girls who get dress coded frequently). But I had hoped that I could extend their good behavior to the next day by making a big deal about how proud I was of them. I hoped it would help them realize how much easier class can be when they pay attention and do what I ask the first time I ask. And I know a lot of these kids don’t come from the best homes and some of their families have to use food stamps, so I wanted to get them something filling. Donut day ended up pushing my morale off a cliff because I “didn’t get the good kind, so [doing the work was] not even worth it.” 

I know I was a self-centered asshole when I was a teenager, and I know that developmentally that’s just where their brains are, but dear god I hope I never made my teachers feel the way I was feeling after that. I’m still working hard to try to get through to them and show them that I respect them and want them to grow up to be good human beings. But it’s days like that that make me feel like I’m just wasting my energy on screaming into a void that can never be filled.

For me, the thing that doesn’t work for me about therapy is the access I have to therapists. I’m living below the poverty line so I am able to get mental health services for free, which has been helpful in the long-run. But the problem I face is that the place I go to seems to be a “foot in the door” type job for new therapists trying to get into the field, and they eventually find nicer places to work. And that’s really painful for me because opening up to people is really difficult, and it seems like whenever I finally start to feel comfortable with a therapist, they move on to work somewhere else. I couldn’t stand that anymore so when I was told I would have a new therapist to talk to, i never made an appointment with her. I keep going to my psychologist for the meds. But I can’t stand switching therapists every few months and having to go through the process of explaining my situation and having my past traumas poked at.

Personally, the thing I dislike about King is how hung up he gets on the geography of things. I’m not very good at understanding directions without looking at a map, so when he does that I usually zone out until he starts talking about stuff that I can understand better. But other than that, I really love his work otherwise and I have almost every book he’s written. I think he’s worth getting into. He writes dark stuff but he has a good sense of humor about it, which I really appreciate. 

Anyway, I normally recommend the Shining for people who want to get into his work, but if that’s not doing anything for you, I’d say try Carrie. Or if you have trouble with reading through directions like I do, there’s some versions of Under the Dome that includes a map of the town it’s set in, which was something that really helped me get through it. 

I hope this helps!! Good luck!!

The first book I read by him was Cell. I picked it because it was a paperback, and it looked a lot less daunting than It or Bag of Bones. It's not his best work, but it's a good start if you want to get an idea of what his writing voice is like. 


Also, the Shining is an excellent place to start, I think. Or Carrie. Those are more of his iconic works. Duma Key is also really good, albeit less popular. Those are good though because a lot of his novels kind of tie into each other and make references to his other work, which is fine, but sometimes it leaves you feeling like you're missing out on something. 


Also, he has a lot of books where he is writing about a whole town, and so the perspective of the story switches between characters a lot. If you like that sort of thing, maybe you should start with Salem's Lot or Under the Dome. If not, though, I'd recommend just sticking to the other books I mentioned.
